'''George McDonald Church''' (born August 28, 1954) is an American [[geneticist]], [[molecular engineering|molecular engineer]], [[chemist]], serial entrepreneur, and pioneer in [[personal genomics]] and [[synthetic biology]].<ref>{{cite web |date=2020-09-20 |title=The Future of Synthetic Biology with Prof. George Church |url=https://www.harvardae.org/new-events/2020/9/22/the-future-of-synthetic-biology-with-george-church#:~:text=About%20George%20Church&text=Church%20is%20known%20for%20pioneering,generation%20sequencing%E2%80%9D%20methods%20and%20companies |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220924151131/https://www.harvardae.org/new-events/2020/9/22/the-future-of-synthetic-biology-with-george-church#:~:text=About%20George%20Church&text=Church%20is%20known%20for%20pioneering,generation%20sequencing%E2%80%9D%20methods%20and%20companies |archive-date=2022-09-24 |access-date=2023-01-12 |website=Harvard Alumni Entrepreneurs}}</ref> He is the Robert Winthrop Professor of Genetics at [[Harvard Medical School]], Professor of [[Harvard–MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology|Health Sciences and Technology]] at [[Harvard University]] and [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], and a founding member of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering]] at [[Harvard University]].<ref name=NairNASbio/><ref name=googlescholar>{{GoogleScholar|id=SfDzdgEAAAAJ}}</ref><ref name=scopus>{{Scopus|id=7005451318}}</ref>

Through his Harvard laboratory, Church has co-founded around 50 biotechnology companies.<ref name="arep.med.harvard.edu">{{cite web |title=Newcos GClab |url=https://arep.med.harvard.edu/gmc/newco.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230113021523/https://arep.med.harvard.edu/gmc/newco.html |archive-date=2023-01-13 |access-date=2023-01-13 |website=[[Harvard Medical School|Harvard Molecular Technologies]]}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=DeFrancesco |first=Laura |date=2020-01-01 |title=One year, 1 lab, 16 spinouts |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-019-0369-7 |journal=Nature Biotechnology |language=en |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=9–13 |doi=10.1038/s41587-019-0369-7 |pmid=31873218 |s2cid=209461325 |issn=1546-1696|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="liebertpub.com">{{cite journal | url=https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/full/10.1089/genbio.2022.29021.gch | doi=10.1089/genbio.2022.29021.gch | title=Thirty-Eight Special: George Church Pushes the Biotech Envelope | journal=Gen Biotechnology | date=April 2022 | volume=1 | issue=2 | pages=127–132 | last1=Church | first1=George M. | last2=Philippidis | first2=Alex | last3=Davies | first3=Kevin | s2cid=248305602| url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 2018, the Church laboratory at Harvard spun off 16 biotechnology companies in one year.<ref name=":0"/>

In 2017, ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine listed him in their list of 100 most influential people in the world.<ref name="Time">{{cite news | url=https://time.com/collection/2017-time-100/4742749/george-church/ | title=George Church: The World's 100 Most Influential People}}</ref> {{as of|2023|January|}}, Church is as a member of the [[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]' Board of Sponsors.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 30, 2017 |title=Board of Sponsors |url=https://thebulletin.org/about-us/board-of-sponsors/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230113035318/https://thebulletin.org/about-us/board-of-sponsors/ |archive-date=2023-01-13 |access-date=2023-01-13 |website=[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Church was born on August 28, 1954, on [[MacDill Air Force Base]] in [[Tampa, Florida]], and grew up in nearby [[Clearwater, Florida]].<ref name=NairNASbio/><ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= George M. Church |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/church-george-m|publisher= [[Science History Institute]]}}</ref><ref name="transcript">{{cite book|first=David C. |last=Brock|title=George M. Church, Transcript of Interviews Conducted by David C. Brock in New Orleans, Louisiana on 3 March 2008 |date=March 3, 2008 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/church_gm_0408_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]]}}</ref><ref name="DuncanNYT10">David Ewing Duncan, 2010, [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/08/science/08church.html "On a Mission to Sequence the Genomes of 100,000 People: The geneticist George Church advises or licenses technology to most companies involved in sequencing"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', June 7, 2010. Retrieved February 26, 2015.</ref> He attended high school at the preparatory boarding school [[Phillips Academy]], in [[Andover, Massachusetts]], from 1968 to 1972.<ref name=SaltonPhil09>Alex Salton, 2009, "Geneticist George Church '72 Sought Independence at PA", ''The Phillipian'', April 17, 2009, see {{cite web |url=https://phillipian.net/articles/geneticist-george-church-72-sought-independence-at-pa |title=The Phillipian |date=April 17, 2009 |access-date=March 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20150228154845/http://phillipian.net/articles/geneticist-george-church-72-sought-independence-at-pa |archive-date=February 28, 2015}}. Retrieved March 2, 2015.</ref> He then attended [[Duke University]], where he obtained a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in [[zoology]] and [[chemistry]] in two years.<ref name=NairNASbio/>

In the fall of 1973, Church began research work at Duke University with assistant professor of [[biochemistry]] [[Sung-Hou Kim]], work that continued a year later in a graduate biochemistry program at Duke on an [[National Science Foundation]] fellowship.<ref name="transcript"/><ref name=MillerNG15/>

As Peter Miller reported on Church for the ''[[National Geographic]]'' series, "The Innovators":{{blockquote|As a graduate student at Duke&nbsp;... he used x-ray crystallography to study the three-dimensional structure of "transfer" RNA, which decodes DNA and carries instructions to other parts of the cell. It was groundbreaking research, but Church spent so much time in the lab—up to a hundred hours a week—that he neglected his other classes [in the fall of 1975].<ref name="MillerNG15">Peter Miller, 2015, "News, The Innovators Project: George Church, The Future Without Limits", ''National Geographic'' (online), see [https://web.archive.org/web/20140604093256/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/innovators/2014/06/140602-george-church-innovation-biology-science-genetics-de-extinction/]. Retrieved 26 February 2015.</ref>}}
As a result, Church was not compliant with Duke graduate academic policies, and was withdrawn from the degree program in January 1976. He was told that "[We] hope that whatever problems&nbsp;... contributed to your lack of success&nbsp;... at Duke will not keep you from a successful pursuit of a productive career."<ref name=MillerNG15/><ref>Duke University Graduate School, Office of the Dean, 1976, [http://arep.med.harvard.edu/gmc/F.jpg "Dear Mr. Church&nbsp;..."], January 16, 1976, private letter from W.G. Katzenmeyer, Associate Dean, to George McDonald Church, in the archives of G.M. Church. Retrieved March 4, 2015.</ref> The work gave rise to publications  including a ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|PNAS]]'' report with Church as lead author on an early model for molecular interactions between the [[minor groove]] of double-stranded [[DNA]] and β-ribbons of proteins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Church |first1=G M |last2=Sussman |first2=J L |last3=Kim |first3=S H |date=1977 |title=Secondary structural complementarity between DNA and proteins. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=74 |issue=4 |pages=1458–1462 |doi=10.1073/pnas.74.4.1458 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=430798 |pmid=266187|bibcode=1977PNAS...74.1458C }}</ref>

Church returned to graduate work at [[Harvard University]] in 1977 under [[Walter Gilbert]],<ref>Jeffrey Perkel, 2013, "BioTechniques: Celebrating 30 Years of Methods Development", ''BioTechniques'' '''55'''(5), November 2013, 227–230, see [http://www.biotechniques.com/BiotechniquesJournal/2013/November/BioTechniques-Celebrating-30-Years-of-Methods-Development/biotechniques-348091.html?service=print] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402090047/http://www.biotechniques.com/BiotechniquesJournal/2013/November/BioTechniques-Celebrating-30-Years-of-Methods-Development/biotechniques-348091.html?service=print|date=April 2, 2015}}. Retrieved March 21, 2014.</ref> and completed a [[Doctor of Science|Ph.D]] in [[biochemistry]] and [[molecular biology]] working on [[mobile genetic elements]] within [[intron]]s of [[Mitochondrion|yeast mitochondrial]] and mouse [[immunoglobulin]] genes (1984).<ref name="churchphd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=George|last=Church |title=Genetic Elements within Yeast Mitochondrial and Mouse Immunoglobulin Introns (Sequence, Enhancer, Technique) |publisher=Harvard University|year=1984 |oclc=13285113|id={{ProQuest|303300427}}}}</ref>

==Career==
After completing his doctoral work, Church spent six months of 1984 at [[Biogen]], the industrial laboratory site where Gilbert had relocated a sizable part of his former Harvard group.<ref name=NairNASbio>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Nair | first1 = P.
| doi = 10.1073/pnas.1204148109
| title = Profile of George M. Church
| journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
| year = 2012
| pmid = 22474375
| pmc =3409755
| volume=109
| issue = 30
| pages=11893–11895
| bibcode = 2012PNAS..10911893N | doi-access = free
}}</ref> This was followed soon after by a [[Life Sciences Research Foundation]] postdoctoral fellowship at the [[University of California, San Francisco]] with [[Gail R. Martin]],<ref>LSRF, 2015, "Resources, 1983 Fellow George Church", see [http://www.lsrf.org/resources/resources-detail-view/1983-fellow-george-church] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712214411/http://www.lsrf.org/resources/resources-detail-view/1983-fellow-george-church|date=July 12, 2018}}. Retrieved February 26, 2015.</ref><ref>LSRF, 2015, "Fellows:Alumni, George Church (1984)", see [http://www.lsrf.org/fellows/alumni]. Retrieved February 26, 2015.</ref> a member of the National Academy of Sciences and joint-discoverer of a technique to extract mouse embryonic stem cells.<ref>Elie Dolgin, 2009, [http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/27244/title/Stem-cell-rat-race/ "Stem cell rat race"], ''[[The Scientist (magazine)|The Scientist]]'', April 1, 2009. Retrieved February 26, 2015.</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Martin G | title = Isolation of a pluripotent cell line from early mouse embryos cultured in medium conditioned by teratocarcinoma stem cells. | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci USA | volume = 78 | issue = 12 | pages = 7634–8 |date=December 1981 | pmid = 6950406 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.78.12.7634 | pmc = 349323|bibcode = 1981PNAS...78.7634M | doi-access = free}}</ref>

Church joined the [[Harvard Medical School]] faculty as an assistant professor in 1986.<ref name=NairNASbio/> Church is now the Robert Winthrop Professor of Genetics at Harvard Medical School,<ref name=LeggBG14>Heidi Legg, 2014, "Harvard Professor George Church and the future of genomics", at ''BetaBoston, a Boston Globe'' site (online), December 25, 2014, see {{cite web |url=https://betaboston.com/news/2014/12/25/harvard-professor-george-church-and-the-future-of-genomics |title=Harvard Professor George Church and the future of genomics &#124; BetaBoston |access-date=March 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150306031724/http://www.betaboston.com/news/2014/12/25/harvard-professor-george-church-and-the-future-of-genomics/ |archive-date=March 6, 2015}}. Retrieved March 2, 2015.</ref> and a member of the Harvard-MIT health sciences and technology faculty. He was also a founding member of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering]] at Harvard University.<ref name=NairNASbio/> He served as the director of the Center of Excellence in Genomic Science (CEGS) at the Harvard Medical School, funded by a P50-type award from the [[National Human Genome Research Institute]] (NHGRI), a part of the [[National Institutes of Health]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Active Centers of Excellence in Genomic Science Awards |url=https://www.genome.gov/sites/default/files/media/files/2020-01/2019_CEGS_Awards.pdf |website=National Human Genome Research Institute}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date= August 5, 2016|title=George Church, Ph.D. |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/team/core-faculty/george-church/ |access-date=2025-11-13 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

He co-founded [[Veritas Genetics]] and its European and Latin American subsidiary, Veritas Intercontinental, with the idea of bringing the benefits of genomic data to millions of people globally.

Church was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2012 for contributions to human genome sequencing technologies and DNA synthesis and assembly.

In 2018, Church co-founded [[Nebula Genomics]], a [[personal genomics]] company that offers a [[whole-genome sequencing]] service.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/press-releases/2020-02-18/nebula-genomics-partnering-with-bgi-sets-industry-standard-by-offering-30x-whole-genome-sequencing-for-299|title=Nebula Genomics, Partnering with BGI, Sets Industry Standard by Offering 30x Whole-Genome Sequencing for $299|date=February 18, 2020|access-date=February 14, 2022|website=[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20220214230142/https://www.bloomberg.com/press-releases/2020-02-18/nebula-genomics-partnering-with-bgi-sets-industry-standard-by-offering-30x-whole-genome-sequencing-for-299|archive-date=February 14, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref> The company says that it is developing its own [[blockchain]], intending to provide free sequencing in exchange for users' genomic and personal data. The decentralized nature of a blockchain also has the potential to improve aspects of data privacy and security, but identification of individuals could still be possible (DNA itself is a unique identifier) and law enforcement could still issue search warrants or subpoena the data.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/genetics-start-up-wants-to-sequence-peoples-genomes-for-free/|title=Genetics Start-Up Wants to Sequence People's Genomes for Free|date=November 17, 2018|access-date=February 14, 2022|website=[[Scientific American]]|last=Weintraub|first=Karen|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210303052546/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/genetics-start-up-wants-to-sequence-peoples-genomes-for-free/|archive-date=March 3, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/story/you-can-soon-get-your-dna-sequenced-anonymously/|title=You Can Soon Get Your DNA Sequenced Anonymously|date=September 19, 2019|access-date=February 14, 2022|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|last=Molteni|first=Megan|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220214180337/https://www.wired.com/story/you-can-soon-get-your-dna-sequenced-anonymously/|archive-date=February 14, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nebulagenomics.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/360036114572-Privacy-Policy|title=Privacy Policy|date=November 21, 2019|access-date=February 14, 2022|website=[[Nebula Genomics]]|last=Quinn|first=Kevin|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203190555/https://nebulagenomics.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/360036114572-Privacy-Policy|archive-date=December 3, 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2021, Church joined as a co-founder of HLTH.network (formerly Shivom),<ref>{{Cite web|title=Genomics Pioneer George Church Becomes Co-Founder of Shivom|url=https://www.pharmiweb.com/press-release/2021-03-31/genomics-pioneer-george-church-becomes-co-founder-of-shivom|access-date=August 17, 2021|website=PharmiWeb.com|language=en}}</ref> a healthcare blockchain startup which created the world's first global genomics data sharing and analytics marketplace. The HLTH.network aims to be the "world's first base layer protocol for global health data."<ref>{{Cite web|title=HLTH – The Global Healthcare Ecosystem|url=https://hlth.network/|access-date=August 17, 2021|website=hlth.network}}</ref> In 2025, Church joined Lila Sciences, an [[AI agent]] platform startup, as Chief Scientist.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-28 |title=Why George Church took chief scientist role at a Cambridge AI startup |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2025/05/28/lila-sciences-george-church.html |access-date= |website=Boston Business Journal |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== George Church Institute of Regenesis: collaboration with BGI Group, China ===
Since 2007, Church has served on the scientific advisory board of [[BGI Group]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-07-02 |title=California rejected Chinese company's push to help with coronavirus testing. Was that the right move? |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/07/02/china-bgi-california-testing/ |access-date=2025-11-13 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

In 2017, BGI established the "George Church Institute of Regenesis", a research collaboration between Church's lab and about a dozen staffers at BGI in China. Dr. Xun Xu, executive director of BGI Group said: 
{{blockquote|Professor George Church is a legend in this field for his creative achievements in gene editing and genome synthesis. With support of advanced technology platform of China National GeneBank, the collaboration between BGI and Professor Church will bring top resources and talents together to overcome current bottleneck issues and further improve the technology.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bio-itworld.com/news/2017/10/27/bgi-launches-george-church-institute | title=BGI Launches George Church Institute }}</ref>}}

On February 18, 2020, Nebula Genomics, a personal genomics company founded by Church,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://nebula.org/george-church/ | title=Meet Prof. George Church &#124; Nebula Genomics}}</ref> announced that had partnered up with BGI; the saliva samples sent to Nebula Genomics for decoding are then sent by the company to BGI labs in Hong Kong for sequencing.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/07/02/china-bgi-california-testing/|title=California rejected Chinese company's push to help with coronavirus testing. Was that the right move?|date=July 2, 2020|access-date=February 14, 2022|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|last1=Whalen|first1=Jeanne|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220214004938/https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/07/02/china-bgi-california-testing/|archive-date=February 14, 2022|url-status=live|last2=Dwoskin|first2=Elizabeth}}</ref> Nebula Genomics said that this partnership was made to bring down the cost of whole-genome sequencing (they offer 30x whole-genome sequencing for $299), since normally it has a cost that makes it inaccessible to most people.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.biospace.com/nebula-genomics-partnering-with-bgi-sets-industry-standard-by-offering-30x-whole-genome-sequencing-for-299|title=Nebula Genomics, Partnering with BGI, Sets Industry Standard by Offering 30x Whole-Genome Sequencing for $299|date=February 18, 2020|access-date=February 14, 2022|website=[[BioSpace]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220118183040/https://www.biospace.com/article/releases/nebula-genomics-partnering-with-bgi-sets-industry-standard-by-offering-30x-whole-genome-sequencing-for-299/|archive-date=January 18, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Research===
====Church and the foundation of genomics====
With [[Walter Gilbert]], Church published the first direct [[genomic sequencing]] method in 1984.<ref name="pmid3463957">{{cite journal |vauthors=Saluz HP, Jiricny J, Jost JP | title = Genomic sequencing reveals a positive correlation between the kinetics of strand-specific DNA demethylation of the overlapping estradiol/glucocorticoid-receptor binding sites and the rate of avian vitellogenin mRNA synthesis | journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. | volume = 83 | issue = 19 | pages = 7167–71 | year = 1986 | pmid = 3463957 | pmc = 386676 | quote = Direct genomic sequencing, first described by Church and Gilbert (15) and further developed in our laboratory (16), overcomes the disadvantages inherent to the use of restriction enzymes. | doi=10.1073/pnas.83.19.7167|bibcode = 1986PNAS...83.7167S | doi-access = free}}</ref> Described in that publication were the cyclic application of fluids to a solid phase alternating with imaging, plus avoidance of bacterial cloning, strategies that are still used in current dominant [[Next-Generation Sequencing]] technologies. These technologies began to affect genome-scale sequencing in 2005.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Shendure J, Porreca GJ, Reppas NB, Lin X, McCutcheon JP, Rosenbaum AM, Wang MD, Zhang K, Mitra RD, Church GM | s2cid = 11405973 | title = Accurate Multiplex Polony Sequencing of an Evolved Bacterial Genome | journal = Science | volume = 309 | issue = 5741 | pages = 1728–32 | year = 2005 | pmid = 16081699 | doi = 10.1126/science.1117389 |bibcode = 2005Sci...309.1728S| doi-access = free }}</ref> Church also helped initiate the [[Human Genome Project]] in 1984.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Cook-Deegan RM | title = The Alta summit, December 1984 | journal = Genomics | volume = 5 | issue = 3 | pages = 661–663 | year = 1989 | pmid = 2613249 | doi = 10.1016/0888-7543(89)90042-6}}</ref> He invented the broadly applied concepts of molecular [[Multiplex (assay)|multiplexing]] and barcode tags,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Church GM, Kieffer-Higgins S | title = Multiplex DNA sequencing | journal = Science | volume = 240 | issue = 4849 | pages = 185–188 | year = 1988 | pmid = 3353714 | doi = 10.1126/science.3353714 |bibcode = 1988Sci...240..185C}}</ref> and his genome was the fifth whole human genome ever sequenced. Church was the first person to make his medical records and genome publicly available to researchers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/changing-america/enrichment/arts-culture/549108-first-genomic-nft-to-be-sold-for-science-and-a|title=First genomic NFT to be sold for science — and a statement|date=April 19, 2021|access-date=February 15, 2022|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|last=Srikanth|first=Anagha|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427213242/https://thehill.com/changing-america/enrichment/arts-culture/549108-first-genomic-nft-to-be-sold-for-science-and-a|archive-date=April 27, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> Technology transfer of automated sequencing and software from his Harvard laboratory to [[Genome Therapeutics Corporation|Genome Therapeutics Corp.]] resulted in the first bacterial genome sequence and first commercial genome (the human [[pathogen]] ''[[Helicobacter pylori]]'') in 1994.<ref name="NG">{{cite journal | title = Capitalizing on the genome | journal = Nature Genetics | volume = 13 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–5 | year = 1996 | pmid = 8673083 | doi = 10.1038/ng0596-1 | doi-access = free}}</ref> Church was co-inventor of [[nanopore]] sequencing in 1995,<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1186/s13059-016-1103-0 | title=The Oxford Nanopore MinION: Delivery of nanopore sequencing to the genomics community | journal=Genome Biology | date=November 25, 2016 | volume=17 | issue=1 | page=239 | last1=Jain | first1=Miten | last2=Olsen | first2=Hugh E. | last3=Paten | first3=Benedict |author4-link=Mark Akeson | last4=Akeson | first4=Mark | pmid=27887629 | pmc=5124260 | doi-access=free }}</ref> which is now commercially available (e.g. [[Oxford Nanopore Technologies]]), but not in the form embodied in Church's contribution to the original patents.<ref>{{cite web|title=Genia Technologies Collaborates with Professors Jingyue Ju at Columbia and George Church at Harvard to Develop a Nanopore-based Sequencing Platform |date=October 3, 2012 |url=http://news.gnom.es/pr/genia-technologies-collaborates-with-professors-jingyue-ju-at-columbia-and-george-church-at-harvard-to-develop-a-nanopore-based-sequencing-platform |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130825022900/http://news.gnom.es/pr/genia-technologies-collaborates-with-professors-jingyue-ju-at-columbia-and-george-church-at-harvard-to-develop-a-nanopore-based-sequencing-platform |archive-date=August 25, 2013}}{{full citation needed|date=July 2014}}</ref>

To aid in the interpretation and sharing of genomes, Church initiated the [[Personal Genome Project]] (PGP) in 2005,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Church GM | title = The Personal Genome Project | journal = Molecular Systems Biology | volume = 1 | issue = 1 | pages = E1–E3 | year = 2005 | article-number = 2005.0030 | pmid = 16729065 | pmc = 1681452 | doi = 10.1038/msb4100040}}</ref> providing the world's only open-access human genome and trait data sets.<ref name=nhgri>{{cite web | url= http://www.genome.gov/27553487 | title= Researchers explore genomic data privacy and risk (NIH NHGRI) | author= Ian L. Marpuri | date= April 8, 2013 | access-date= June 9, 2013 | archive-date= May 27, 2013 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130527225849/https://www.genome.gov/27553487 }}</ref><ref name=angrist /><ref name=pg /> Eight trios (mother, father, and child) from the Personal Genome Project are in the process of being chosen to act as the primary genome standards (reference materials) for the NIST+FDA genomeinabottle.org program.<ref>{{cite news |publisher= NGS Leaders |title= Okay, You've Sequenced My Genome: Are You Sure You Got it Right? |url= http://www.ngsleaders.org/Blog/Okay,-You-ve-Sequenced-My-Genome--Are-You-Sure-You-Got-it-Right-/ |access-date= June 9, 2013 |archive-date= July 5, 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130705054215/http://www.ngsleaders.org/Blog/Okay,-You-ve-Sequenced-My-Genome--Are-You-Sure-You-Got-it-Right-/? }}</ref>

Church furthermore announced his intention to publish his DNA via NFT and use the profits made through its sale to finance research conducted by Nebula Genomics. In June 2022 20 NFTs with his likeness were published instead of the originally planned NFTs of his DNA due to the market conditions at the time.<ref name="jonesnature">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Nicola |date=2021-06-18 |title=How scientists are embracing NFTs |journal=Nature |volume=594 |issue= 7864|pages=481–482 |doi=10.1038/d41586-021-01642-3|pmid=34145410 |bibcode=2021Natur.594..481J |s2cid=235481285 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Despite leading to mixed reactions the project is considered to be part of an effort to use the genetic data of 15,000 individuals to support genetic research. By using NFTs the project wants to ensure that the users submitting their genetic data are able to receive direct payment for their contributions.<ref name="jonesnature"/><ref>{{cite web|access-date=2023-02-21|first=Victor |last=Tangermann|date=2022-04-21|title=A Harvard Scientist is Selling his Genetic Code as an NFT|url=https://futurism.com/neoscope/george-church-harvard-scientist-genetic-code-nft|website=Neoscope ― Futurism}}</ref>

====Synthetic biology and genome engineering====
Church has co-developed "genome engineering" technologies since 1997 via either general homologous recombination (recA and lambda-red) or via sequence-specific nucleases.{{cn|date=October 2026}} Since 2004, his team has developed the use of [[DNA array]] (aka DNA chip) synthesizers for combinatorial libraries and assembling large genome segments.{{cn|date=October 2026}} He co-developed Multiplex Automated Genome Engineering (MAGE) and optimized [[CRISPR]]/[[Cas9]], discovered by [[Jennifer Doudna]] and [[Emmanuelle Charpentier]] for engineering a variety of genomes ranging from yeast to human.{{cn|date=October 2026}} His laboratory's use of CRISPR in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPS) is the latest contender for precise gene therapy.<ref>{{cite magazine | title=This Protein Could Change Biotech Forever | author= Matthew Herper | date=March 19, 2013 | magazine=[[Forbes]] | url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/matthewherper/2013/03/19/the-protein-that-could-change-biotech-forever/}}</ref>

His team is the first to tackle a genome-scale change in the genetic code. This was done in a 4.7&nbsp;million basepair genome of an industrially useful microbe (''E. coli'') with the goal of making a safer and more productive strain; this strain uses [[non-proteinogenic amino acids]] in proteins, and is metabolically and genetically isolated from other species.{{cn|date=October 2026}}

He has co-invented several uses for DNA, including detectors for [[dark matter]] – [[Weakly interacting massive particles]] (WIMPs),<ref>{{cite magazine | title=Revolutionary 'DNA Tracking Chamber' Could Detect Dark Matter |magazine=[[MIT Technology Review]] |date= July 2, 2012 | url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2012/07/02/255644/revolutionary-dna-tracking-chamber-could-detect-dark-matter/}}</ref> anti-cancer "nano-robots",<ref>{{cite news | publisher=Physics World | title= DNA nanorobot delivers drugs | url = http://physicsworld.com/cws/article/news/2012/feb/17/dna-nanorobot-delivers-drugs |date=February 17, 2012 | author=Belle Dumé}}</ref> and strategies for digital data storage that are over a million times denser than conventional disk drives.<ref>{{cite news | first=Robert Lee |last=Hotz | title= Future of Data: Encoded in DNA | newspaper=The Wall Street Journal | date= August 16, 2012 | url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10000872396390444233104577593291643488120?mod=djemalertNEWS}}</ref> Together with polymerase, DNA can be used to sense and store variation in photons, nucleotides, or ions.<ref name=Neuron2012/>

====The BRAIN initiative====
Church was part of a team who, in a 2012 scientific commentary, proposed a Brain Activity Map, later named [[BRAIN Initiative]] (Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies).<ref name=Neuron2012/><ref>{{cite news | title=Obama Seeking to Boost Study of Human Brain | newspaper= The New York Times | author = John Markoff | date = February 17, 2013 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/02/18/science/project-seeks-to-build-map-of-human-brain.html}}</ref>
They outlined specific experimental techniques that might be used to achieve what they termed a "functional [[connectome]]", as well as new technologies that will have to be developed in the course of the project,<ref name=Neuron2012>{{cite journal |vauthors=Alivisatos AP, Chun M, Church GM, Greenspan RJ, Roukes ML, Yuste R |title=The Brain Activity Map Project and the Challenge of Functional Connectomics |journal=[[Neuron (journal)|Neuron]] |volume=74 |issue=6 |pages=970–974 |date=June 2012 |pmid=22726828 |pmc=3597383 |doi=10.1016/j.neuron.2012.06.006}}</ref> including wireless, minimally invasive methods to detect and manipulate neuronal activity, either utilizing [[microelectronics]] or [[synthetic biology]]. In one such proposed method, enzymatically produced [[DNA]] would serve as a "ticker tape record" of neuronal activity.<ref name=Neuron2012/><ref name=PlosONE>{{cite journal |vauthors=Zamft BM, Marblestone AH, Kording K, Schmidt D, Martin-Alarcon D, Tyo K, Boyden ES, Church G | title = Measuring Cation Dependent DNA Polymerase Fidelity Landscapes by Deep Sequencing | journal = [[PLoS ONE]] | volume = 7 | issue = 8 | date = August 2012 | pmid = 22928047 | pmc = 3425509 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0043876 | article-number=e43876|bibcode = 2012PLoSO...743876Z | doi-access = free}}</ref>

====Gene therapy, ageing, and age reversal====
Church worked on engineered adeno-associated viral vectors to evade innate immune and inflammatory responses. The research was published in ''Science Translational Medicine'' in 2021 and showed the possibility of a less immunogenic gene therapy with the new TLR9-edited Adeno-associated viruses (AAV) as a safer viral vector.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1126/scitranslmed.abd3438 | title=Engineering adeno-associated viral vectors to evade innate immune and inflammatory responses | year=2021 | last1=Chan | first1=Ying Kai | last2=Wang | first2=Sean K. | last3=Chu | first3=Colin J. | last4=Copland | first4=David A. | last5=Letizia | first5=Alexander J. | last6=Costa Verdera | first6=Helena | last7=Chiang | first7=Jessica J. | last8=Sethi | first8=Meher | last9=Wang | first9=May K. | last10=Neidermyer | first10=William J. | last11=Chan | first11=Yingleong | last12=Lim | first12=Elaine T. | last13=Graveline | first13=Amanda R. | last14=Sanchez | first14=Melinda | last15=Boyd | first15=Ryan F. | last16=Vihtelic | first16=Thomas S. | last17=Inciong | first17=Rolando Gian Carlo O. | last18=Slain | first18=Jared M. | last19=Alphonse | first19=Priscilla J. | last20=Xue | first20=Yunlu | last21=Robinson-Mccarthy | first21=Lindsey R. | last22=Tam | first22=Jenny M. | last23=Jabbar | first23=Maha H. | last24=Sahu | first24=Bhubanananda | last25=Adeniran | first25=Janelle F. | last26=Muhuri | first26=Manish | last27=Tai | first27=Phillip W. ====Space biology and space genetics====
Church is a faculty member in the ''Consortium of Space Genetics'' at [[Harvard Medical School]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://spacegenetics.hms.harvard.edu/people/george-church-phd | title=George M. Church, Ph.D. &#124; Consortium for Space Genetics | access-date=September 6, 2022 | archive-date=September 25, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220925141914/https://spacegenetics.hms.harvard.edu/people/george-church-phd }}</ref>

====De-extinction, woolly mammoth revival project, and Colossal Biosciences====
In March 2015, Church and his genetics research team at Harvard successfully copied some [[woolly mammoth]] genes into the genome of an Asian elephant. Using the [[CRISPR]] DNA editing technique, his group spliced genetic segments from frozen mammoth specimens, including genes from the ears, subcutaneous fat, and hair attributes, into the DNA of skin cells from a modern elephant. ''[[National Geographic]]'', in an article titled "''Mammoth-elephant hybrids could be created within the decade. Should they be?''", reported: 
{{blockquote|Church's dreams of engineering a hybrid mammoth first deepened after an interview he did with the New York Times in 2008 about efforts to sequence the woolly mammoth genome.}}

This marked the first time that woolly mammoth genes had been functionally active since the species became extinct.<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.popsci.com/woolly-mammoth-dna-brought-life-elephant-cells |title=Woolly Mammoth DNA Successfully Spliced into Elephant Cells |author=Sarah Fecht |date=March 24, 2014 |publisher=[[Popular Science]]}}</ref> Their work has not been subject to peer review, however. Church stated that "Just making a DNA change isn't that meaningful. We want to read out the phenotypes." To do that, the team plans to perform further tests to get the hybrid cells into becoming specialized tissues, and from there attempting to turn the hybrid elephant/mammoth skin cells into hybrid embryos that can be grown in [[artificial womb]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Harvard Wyss Institute and Colossal Foundation Advance Artificial Womb Tech {{!}} EdTech News |url=https://www.edtechinnovationhub.com/news/harvards-wyss-institute-and-colossal-foundation-partner-on-artificial-womb-research-for-conservation |access-date=2025-04-21 |website=EdTech Innovation Hub |language=en-GB}}</ref>

On September 13, 2021, Church founded a biosciences and genetics company, [[Colossal Biosciences]], with entrepreneur [[Ben Lamm]]. The company is attempting to use genetic code to revive the woolly mammoth by equipping [[Asian elephants]] with mammoth traits.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/mammoth-elephant-hybrids-could-be-created-within-the-decade-should-they-be|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210913145249/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/mammoth-elephant-hybrids-could-be-created-within-the-decade-should-they-be|archive-date=September 13, 2021|author=Michael Greshko|title=Mammoth-elephant hybrids could be created within the decade. Should they be?|date=September 13, 2021|work=National Geographic}}</ref><ref name="nytimes">{{Cite web |last=Zimmer |first=Carl |date=September 13, 2021 |title=A New Company With a Wild Mission: Bring Back the Woolly Mammoth |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/13/science/colossal-woolly-mammoth-DNA.html |access-date=October 26, 2021 |website=The New York Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Laetitia Garriott de Cayeux]], founder-CEO of Global Space Ventures and an investor in Colossal Biosciences, said: 
{{blockquote|In 2014, I asked my friend [[Elon Musk]] who he knew who was poised to make profound changes in the field of genomics, and he said: George Church. So in June 2014, I visited George at his lab in Boston. I immediately knew I'd be looking for an opportunity to collaborate with George. Global Space Ventures is excited to be backing Colossal.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://colossal.com/company/ | title=The Science of Genetics. The Business of Discovery| date=August 6, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://globalspace.ventures/2021/09/13/global-space-ventures-backs-colossals-seed-round/ | title=Global Space Ventures backs Colossal's seed round | work=Global Space Ventures | date=13 September 2021 | access-date=September 6, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220930095541/https://globalspace.ventures/2021/09/13/global-space-ventures-backs-colossals-seed-round/ | archive-date=September 30, 2022 | url-status=dead}}</ref>}}In 2013, in response to a question from ''[[Der Spiegel]]'', Church speculated that it could be technically possible to make a [[Neanderthal]] by reconstructing its DNA and modifying living human cells accordingly.<ref>{{cite magazine |date=January 18, 2013 |title=How DNA will be construction material of the future |url=http://www.spiegel.de/international/zeitgeist/george-church-explains-how-dna-will-be-construction-material-of-the-future-a-877634.html |magazine=[[Der Spiegel]]}}</ref> Translation issues and misreporting led some media outlets to believe that Church was working on such a project and searching for a surrogate mother, causing controversy.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-01-25 |title=Cloned Cave Baby Lost in Translation |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/neanderthal-baby-spawns-debunking-fest |access-date=2025-11-13 |website=PBS News |language=en-us}}</ref> Church clarified that he was not.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Gary J. Remal |date=January 22, 2013 |title=Harvard professor blasts Neanderthal clone baby rumor on Web |url=http://bostonherald.com/news_opinion/local_coverage/2013/01/harvard_professor_blasts_neanderthal_clone_baby_rumor_web |journal=Boston Herald}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |date=January 23, 2013 |title=Spiegel responds to brouhaha over neanderthal clone |url=http://www.spiegel.de/international/spiegel-responds-to-brouhaha-over-neanderthal-clone-interview-a-879311.html |magazine=Der Spiegel}}</ref>

In 2025, Colossal reported the live birth of two "dire wolves" where gray wolf cells received 20 unique gene edits, including 15 edits that directly matched dire wolf DNA and notably an edit that re-introduced pale coat color.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kluger |first=Jeffrey |date=April 7, 2025 |title=The Return of the Dire Wolf |url=https://time.com/7274542/colossal-dire-wolf/}}</ref> That August, Church founded an [[artificial intelligence]] company, [[Astromech (company)|Astromech]], with Lamm.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sechler |first1=Bob |last2=Wistrom |first2=Brent |title=Colossal Biosciences co-founders raise funds for new biology-focused AI startup |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/austin/news/2025/08/14/astromech-colossal-biosciences-ai-austin-biology.html |website=Austin Business Journal |date=14 August 2025}}</ref>

Daugharthy).<ref>{{Cite web |title=10x Genomics Signs Agreement to Acquire ReadCoor |url=http://www.technologynetworks.com/genomics/product-news/10x-genomics-signs-agreement-to-acquire-readcoor-341327 |access-date=March 10, 2022 |website=Genomics Research from Technology Networks |language=en}}</ref>

====Support of open consent====
Church spearheaded the concept and implementation of open access sequencing hardware<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.polonator.org/ | title=Open, Affordable Sequencing | access-date=May 25, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521212447/http://polonator.org/ | archive-date=May 21, 2013}}</ref> and shareable human medical data.<ref name=pg>{{cite web |url=http://PersonalGenomes.org/ | title=Personal Genome Project | access-date=May 25, 2013}}</ref> He has noted the potential for re-identification of human research participants and the tendency for consent forms to be opaque – proposing an alternative "open consent" mechanism.<ref name=nhgri /><ref name=angrist /> He has participated in the Presidential Commission for the Study of Bioethical Issues,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tvworldwide.com/events/bioethics/100708/default.cfm?id=12577&type=flv&test=0&live=0 |title=Presidential Commission for the Study of Bioethical Issues |date=July 8, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014153749/http://www.tvworldwide.com/events/bioethics/100708/default.cfm?id=12577&type=flv&test=0&live=0 |archive-date=October 14, 2013}}</ref> cautioning about the risk of synthetic DNA and proposing risk-reduction via licensing and surveillance.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://arep.med.harvard.edu/SBP/Church_Biohazard04c.htm | title=A Synthetic Biohazard Non-proliferation Proposal | access-date=May 25, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Church G | title = Let us go forth and safely multiply | journal = Nature | volume = 438 | issue = 7067 | page = 423 | date = November 24, 2005 | pmid = 16306966 | doi = 10.1038/438423a |bibcode = 2005Natur.438..423C | s2cid = 4318315 | doi-access = free}}</ref> His laboratory has a major bio-safety engineering focus.<ref name=fi>{{cite journal |vauthors=Isaacs FJ, Carr PA, Wang HH, Lajoie MJ, Sterling B, Kraal L, Tolonen AC, Gianoulis TA, Goodman DB, Reppas NB, Emig CJ, Bang D, Hwang SJ, Jewett MC, Jacobson JM, Church GM | title = Precise Manipulation of Chromosomes in vivo Enables Genome-wide Codon Replacement | journal = Science | volume = 333 | issue = 6040 | pages = 348–53 | year = 2011 | pmid = 21764749 | pmc = 5472332 | doi = 10.1126/science.1205822 |bibcode = 2011Sci...333..348I}}</ref>

Church's detailed online register of funding sources showed that he received funding totaling $686,000 from the nonprofit [[Jeffrey Epstein VI Foundation]] from 2005 to 2007. In 2008, after Jeffrey Epstein′s first conviction, Harvard University′s then president [[Drew Gilpin Faust]] held that the university were no longer to accept gifts from him, yet Epstein continued to help Church to raise funds after serving his prison sentence.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 2020 |title=Report Concerning Jeffrey E. Epstein's Connections to Harvard University |url=https://ogc.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum12481/files/ogc/files/report_concerning_jeffrey_e._epsteins_connections_to_harvard_university.pdf |access-date=2026-02-04 |website=Harvard University |language=en-US}}, pp. 10–13.</ref> Church said in 2019 that he regrets he did not know more about the donor.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-12-08 |title=Scientist George Church talks about accepting donations from Jeffrey Epstein |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/harvard-scientist-george-church-talks-about-accepting-donations-from-jeffrey-epstein-60-minutes-2019-12-08/ |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=CBS News |language=en-US}}</ref> 
[[File:George Church at TED.jpg|thumb| 200px|right|Church at [[TED (conference)|TED 2010]], picture by Steve Jurvetson]]

====Support of open education====
Church is an advisor to the [[Personal Genetics Education Project]]<ref>{{cite web | url=http://pged.org | title= Personal Genetics Education Project | access-date=May 25, 2013}}</ref> and has spent a day teaching at The Jemicy School.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://intranet.synberc.org/outreach/jemicy-school-dyslexia-david-malin-lecture |title=Jemicy School for Dyslexia, David Malin Lecture |date=November 11, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014093526/http://intranet.synberc.org/outreach/jemicy-school-dyslexia-david-malin-lecture |archive-date=October 14, 2013}}</ref> He has promoted citizen science, especially in the fields of synthetic biology and personal genomics.<ref name=angrist>{{cite journal | author = Angrist M | title = Eyes wide open: the Personal Genome Project, citizen science and veracity in informed consent | journal = Personalized Medicine | volume = 6 | issue = 6 | pages = 691–699 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 22328898 | pmc = 3275804 | doi = 10.2217/pme.09.48}}</ref> Since 2008, his team has been hosting an annual Genomes, Environments and Traits (GET) Conference with free online videos.<ref>{{cite web | title=Genomes, Environments and Traits (GET) Conference | url=http://fora.tv/conference/get_conference_2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130420123630/http://fora.tv/conference/get_conference_2013 | url-status=usurped | archive-date=April 20, 2013 | access-date=May 25, 2013}}</ref>

====Rapid Deployment Vaccine Collaborative====
Church is a member of the [[Rapid Deployment Vaccine Collaborative]] (RaDVaC), a group formed early in the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic to create an easily produced, free and open-source vaccine for self-administration.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Some scientists are taking a DIY coronavirus vaccine, and nobody knows if it's legal or if it works|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2020/07/29/1005720/george-church-diy-coronavirus-vaccine/|access-date=March 15, 2021|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Popular science==
Church authored the 2012 ''[[New Scientist]]'s'' "top science book", ''Regenesis: How Synthetic Biology Will Reinvent Nature and Ourselves'' with [[Ed Regis (author)|Ed Regis]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Church George |title= Regenesis |publisher=Basic Books |location=New York |year=2012 | isbn=978-0-465-02175-8}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine | magazine=[[New Scientist]] | url=https://www.newscientist.com/blogs/culturelab/2012/12/the-top-10-science-books-of-2012.html | title=The top 10 science books of 2012}}</ref> He appeared on popular TV shows including [[The Colbert Report]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Church Lab News | access-date=September 8, 2010 | url=http://arep.med.harvard.edu/gmc/news.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Harley|first1=Liz|title=When George Church met Stephen Colbert|url=http://www.frontlinegenomics.com/rich-media/5096/5096-2/|access-date=December 26, 2016|date=May 18, 2016|archive-date=December 27, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161227060818/http://www.frontlinegenomics.com/rich-media/5096/5096-2/}}</ref>

In 2015, [[Jeneen Interlandi]] wrote an article on Church for ''[[Popular Science]]'' titled "''The Church Of George Church: From reviving extinct species to hunting for dark matter, can a single scientist transform biology—and our lives?''", where she states:

{{blockquote|Like an engineer, he (George Church) tends to see the universe not as a disparate set of mysteries but as a machine with a vast array of buttons and levers, each begging to be pushed and pulled.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.popsci.com/church-george-church/ | title=The Church of George Church | date=27 May 2015}}</ref>}}

==Awards and honors==
Church has received accolades including election to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (in 2011),<ref name=NairNASbio/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://nas.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=News_May_3_2011_member_election |title=National Academy of Sciences Members and Foreign Associates Elected |year=2011 |publisher=National Academies |access-date=February 17, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120301195556/http://nas.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=News_May_3_2011_member_election |archive-date=March 1, 2012}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (in 2012).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=02092012 |title= National Academy of Engineering Elects 66 Members and 10 Foreign Associates |year=2012 |publisher=National Academies |access-date=February 17, 2012}}</ref> He received the [[American Society for Microbiology]] Promega Biotechnology Research Award and the [[Bower Award and Prize for Achievement in Science]] of the [[Franklin Institute]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fi.edu/franklinawards/11/bowersci.html |title=Bower Award and Prize for Achievement in Science |year=2011 |publisher=Franklin Institute |access-date=December 23, 2011 |archive-date=March 26, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110326144445/http://www.fi.edu/franklinawards/11/bowersci.html }}</ref> He authored the ''NewScientist'' "top science book", ''Regenesis'' (on synthetic biology) with [[Ed Regis (author)|Ed Regis]].

Other honors include the Triennial International Steven Hoogendijk Award in 2010 and the Scientific American Top 50 twice (for "Designing artificial life" in 2005 and "The $1000 genome" in 2006).<ref>{{cite web | title=American Society for Microbiology honors George M. Church | date=June 8, 2009 | url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2009-06/asfm-asf_7060809.php | access-date=June 9, 2013 | archive-date=February 19, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219223943/http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2009-06/asfm-asf_7060809.php }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=International Steven Hoogendijk Award |year=2010 |url=http://www.bataafschgenootschap.nl/Int%20Steven%20Hoogendijk%20Award |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515100332/http://www.bataafschgenootschap.nl/Int%20Steven%20Hoogendijk%20Award |archive-date=May 15, 2013}}</ref> ''[[Newsweek]]'' picked Church for their 2008 "Power of Ideas" recognition in the category of Medicine (for the Personal Genome Project).<ref>{{cite magazine | url= http://www.thedailybeast.com/newsweek/2008/12/19/the-power-of-ideas.html | title=The Power of Ideas | magazine=[[Newsweek]] | date=December 19, 2008}}</ref> In September 2010, Church was honored for his work in genetics with the Mass High Tech All-Star Award.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://masshightech.bizjournals.com/masshightech/event/26971 |title=All-Star Awards |publisher=Mass High Tech |date=September 8, 2010 |access-date=September 8, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100902141927/http://masshightech.bizjournals.com/masshightech/event/26971 |archive-date=September 2, 2010}}</ref>

He is a member of the Research Advisory Board of [[SENS Research Foundation]].<ref name=SRF2013>{{cite web|last1=Zealley|first1=Ben|title=SRF's Research Advisory Board Welcomes Dr. George Church|url=http://www.sens.org/research/research-blog/srfs-research-advisory-board-welcomes-dr-george-church|access-date=August 18, 2014|date=March 7, 2013}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Church is married to fellow Harvard Medical School faculty member in genetics [[Ting Wu]].<ref>{{cite news |title= Do inventors get enough respect in science? | url=http://www.boston.com/news/science/blogs/science-in-mind/2013/07/02/inventors-get-enough-respect-science/i7wCB2NWW5Ii98XLoO69nL/blog.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130715075830/http://www.boston.com/news/science/blogs/science-in-mind/2013/07/02/inventors-get-enough-respect-science/i7wCB2NWW5Ii98XLoO69nL/blog.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 15, 2013 | work=[[The Boston Globe]] | date=February 7, 2013}}</ref>

Church has been outspoken in his support of following a [[veganism|vegan]] lifestyle, for reasons concerned with health, and with environmental and moral issues. When asked about his dietary choice, Church replied, "I've been [[Veganism|vegan]] off-and-on since 1974 when I was inspired by participating in an MIT nutritional study, and quite strictly since 2004." He goes on to elaborate 4 reasons:{{blockquote|medical ([[cholesterol]] in fish & dairy), energy conservation (up to 20-fold impact), cruelty ("[[organic food|organic]]" animals are deprived of medicines that humans use), and risks of spreading pathogens (not just the flu)&nbsp;... [noting that] veganism is an issue for which personal and global love of life, health and wealth align. It's a pity to lose parts of our humanity and planet just due to a lack of recipes.<ref>{{cite web|title=George Church |url=http://www.veganpeace.com/famousvegans/profiles/george_church.htm |access-date=20 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130118055438/http://www.veganpeace.com/famousvegans/profiles/george_church.htm |archive-date=18 January 2013}}</ref>}}

George identifies as a sentientist.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Church |first1=George |title=A Bill of Rights for the Age of Artificial Intelligence |url=https://onezero.medium.com/a-bill-of-rights-for-the-age-of-artificial-intelligence-d9b1c0e80bac |website=Medium |date=February 12, 2019 |publisher=OneZero}}</ref> [[Sentientism]] is a naturalistic worldview that grants moral consideration to all sentient beings.

In the context of the Personal Genome Project, journalists at ''[[Forbes]]'' and ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' have noted Church's openness about his health issues, including [[dyslexia]], [[narcolepsy]], and high cholesterol (one of the motivations for his vegan diet).<ref name="herper">{{cite magazine | author=Herper, Matthew | title= Going To Church | magazine=Forbes |date= April 27, 2009 |url= https://www.forbes.com/forbes/2009/0427/020-biofuels-biotech-genetics-ideas-opinions.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url = https://www.wired.com/2008/07/ff-church/ |title = How the Personal Genome Project Could Unlock the Mysteries of Life |author= Thomas Goetz |date=July 8, 2008 |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]}}</ref> Church has many of his best ideas during the brief naps caused by his narcolepsy, and therefore does not treat it.<ref>{{Cite web |last=French |first=Kristen |date=2023-01-25 |title=The Creative Sweet Spot of Dreaming |url=https://nautil.us/narcoleptic-naps-are-a-creative-sweet-spot-259482/ |access-date=2024-06-27 |website=Nautilus |language=en-US}}</ref>

Church collaborated with [[transhumanist]] entrepreneur [[James Clement (entrepreneur)|James Clement]] on the Supercentenarian Research Study, which aims to sequence the genomes of [[supercentenarian]]s in hopes of discovering potential genetic factors behind their [[Longevity#Genetics|longevity]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Harmon|first=Amy|date=November 13, 2017|title=The Secret to Long Life? It May Lurk in the DNA of the Oldest Among Us|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/11/13/health/supercentenarians-genetics-longevity.html|access-date=April 10, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> As of 2023, he is part of the [[Enhanced Games]] scientific and ethical advisory commission.<ref name="The Enhanced Olympics: Drugs welcome!">{{cite news |last1=Bailey |first1=Ronald|author-link=Ronald Bailey (writer) |title=The Enhanced Olympics: Drugs welcome! |url=https://reason.com/2023/06/29/the-enhanced-olympics-drugs-welcome/ |access-date=8 July 2023 |work=[[Reason (magazine)|Reason]] |date=29 June 2023}}</ref><ref name="Games on steroids?">{{cite news |last1=Kamath |first1=Amit |title=Games on steroids? Inside an Indian-origin man's plan to organise Enhanced Games |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/sports/sport-others/games-on-steroids-inside-an-indian-origin-mans-plan-to-organise-enhanced-games-8822235/ |access-date=10 July 2023 |work=[[The Indian Express]] |date=9 July 2023 |language=en}}</ref>
